query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The resistance of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the dynamic formation and self-healing of a mechanically robust, passivating surface film enriched in corrosion‐resistant elements. This film, produced by selective oxidation of specific alloying elements at fresh wear surfaces, protects the alloy during concurrent mechanical abrasion and chemical attack.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous high-entropy alloy with a solid solution microstructure that contains elements capable of forming stable, protective oxides (e.g., Cr, Al, Ni).
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to a combined mechanical abrasion (wear) and corrosive environment (such as an acidic electrolyte or molten salt with oxygen presence) that simulates harsh service conditions.
generation.conditions: Controlled tribocorrosion tests where the alloy is subjected to simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosion, with parallel experiments for wear-only and corrosion-only conditions to serve as baselines; oxygen or oxidizing conditions must be maintained to allow passive film formation.
generation.structural_mediator: A passivating surface film (oxide layer) formed via selective oxidation of certain alloying elements.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical abrasion, the alloy’s surface is continuously renewed exposing fresh material. In the presence of a corrosive medium with available oxygen, specific alloying elements oxidize preferentially to form a thin, adherent and self-healing oxide film that acts as a barrier to both further mechanical damage and chemical dissolution. This dynamically regenerating film provides synergistic protection, reducing overall degradation under combined wear-corrosion conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA with the ability to form a robust, self-healing passive film will exhibit lower combined material loss, reduced wear track depth, and lower corrosion rates compared to an identically processed baseline alloy that lacks this selective surface enrichment. The protective effect should result in improved performance during tribocorrosion tests relative to wear-only or corrosion-only baselines.
generation.baseline: A matched high-entropy alloy (or conventional alloy) that does not form—or has its ability to form—a passivating film suppressed, resulting in higher rates of wear and corrosion when exposed to simultaneous degradation conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds under conditions where there is sufficient oxygen (or oxidizing species) to support film formation and where the mechanical load does not exceed the film’s ability to self-repair. In environments that are extremely anoxic or subject the material to loads high enough to prevent the film from reforming, the protective mechanism may fail.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of film formation, the quantitative contribution of each element to the formation and stability of the protective oxide, and the thresholds of mechanical input beyond which the film fails remain uncertain and require further experimental clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a set of tribocorrosion tests on two sets of HEA samples: one that contains the full suite of alloying elements needed for passive film formation, and a modified version where key film-forming elements are reduced or substituted. Samples will be subjected to identical combined wear and corrosion conditions while monitoring in situ surface changes using electron microscopy and surface analysis techniques (e.g., XPS, scanning Kelvin probe).
measurements: Surface film composition and thickness (via XPS or similar)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the full-composition and modified samples show statistically similar degradation rates and surface characteristics—i.e., if the full-composition HEA does not exhibit the formation of a robust, self-healing passive film or improved wear-corrosion resistance compared to the baseline—then the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
